extracted.intended_audience: agency officials, rulemaking counsel, policymakers, and administrative law scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic framework for agencies on identifying, assessing, and responding to mass, malattributed, and computer-generated public comments in rulemaking records, including legal standards, policy concerns, and practical processing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working definition of a mass comment response
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no accepted definition of a “mass comment response,” and the report adopts a working definition based on interviews with agency officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between spontaneous large-volume responses and organized campaigns; recognize that mass responses increase duplicativeness and can stem from lower costs of electronic submission. The report uses a working definition for analytic purposes rather than a fixed statutory meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mass comment campaign (distinguished from mass response)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mass comment campaign is a special case of a mass comment response in which an individual or organization successfully urges a large number of individuals to file comments that express a similar set of views or positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical characteristics include identical or nearly identical language, a posted sample comment, and optional encouragement to add a personalizing sentence. Where solicitations encourage substantively similar but unique comments, it can be difficult to disentangle campaigns from spontaneous mass responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malattributed comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments falsely attributed to persons by whom they were not in fact submitted (false names, nonexistent persons, or persons unaware of the submission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malattribution is facilitated by access to large datasets of personal information and automation tools (e.g., using DMV or voter registration data). The focus is on the false identity issue distinct from other false statements in comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-generated comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments generated by a software algorithm that replace human content generation and human interaction with the agency; once automated, the creator need not further engage and software can repeatedly submit comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary NLP algorithms can produce text difficult to distinguish from human writing (e.g., GPT-3). Computer-generated comments could overwhelm agencies with arbitrarily large numbers of human-quality comments; many current examples are crude and detectable, but technological advances raise detection and volume risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information value: technical/operational vs. preference information
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish two kinds of useful comment content: (1) technical/operational information (scientific studies, data, analysis about implementation and consequences) and (2) expressions of preference or conclusions about desirability of a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/operational information is most valuable for improving rule quality and anticipating consequences. Expressions of preference may be appropriate only in certain contexts (debated among scholars); agencies should consider relevance and statutory limits when weighing preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal limits on information agencies may consider (State Farm/Whitman)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are substantive limits on the kinds of information agencies may consider; under State Farm, an agency is arbitrary and capricious if it relies on factors Congress did not intend it to consider; Whitman example: EPA may not consider costs when setting certain air quality standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must ensure that comment-derived considerations are within statutory authority; public preferences about matters statutorily off-limits (e.g., costs where Congress disallows consideration) are not relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of comment content
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is valuable only if accurate; false or erroneous statements in comments are at least a delay and distraction and, if undiscovered and important, could affect a final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies' expertise often allows recognition of substantive errors, and broad participation can counter misinformation; nonetheless, identification and correction of false submissions require resources and can affect rule quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy: procedural fairness (voice, respectful treatment, explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive (sociological) legitimacy depends on public acceptance, and perceptions of procedural fairness—especially 'voice' (chance to present views and indication input was considered), polite/respectful treatment, and explanations—are key determinants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice-and-comment maps onto 'voice'; agencies should provide indications that input was considered to bolster perceived fairness. Mass, malattributed, or computer-generated comments can undermine perceptions of voice even if agencies can sort them out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy: outcome-oriented concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive legitimacy also derives from outcomes—high-quality, effective decisionmaking increases public acceptance; if technology-enabled comments reduce regulatory quality, legitimacy may erode over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should consider how comment-processing practices affect both perceptions and real quality of regulatory outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing costs and resource burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing, analyzing, and responding to comments consumes time and staff resources; as comment volume grows, processing costs increase (including hiring contractors), and identifying malattributed or computer-generated comments adds further expense and delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should weigh informational and legitimacy benefits of comments against processing costs and consider resource allocation strategies for high-volume rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality/significance threshold for agency response (Home Box Office / Portland Cement / MCI WorldCom)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are required to consider the substance of comments but only need to respond to comments that, if true, raise points relevant to the agency's decision and would require a change in the proposed rule; comments must surpass a materiality threshold before lack of response becomes problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have stated that agencies are not obliged to respond to every comment—only those that challenge a fundamental premise or disclose a factual/policy basis requiring response. Purely speculative or insubstantial comments need not be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to respond in a reasoned manner to significant comments
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must 'respond in a reasoned manner to the comments received, to explain how the agency resolved any significant problems raised by the comments, and to show how that resolution led the agency to the ultimate rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comments raise significant problems, the agency's explanatory response must connect resolution of those problems to the rationale for the final rule (Action on Smoking & Health and related precedents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number/volume of comments is generally not dispositive ('not a vote')
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a broad consensus that the comment process is not a vote; agencies are under 'no obligation to take the approach advocated by the largest number of commenters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts sometimes note comment numbers in context, volume alone does not determine adequacy of agency consideration or correctness of outcome; agencies should focus on substance and relevance rather than sheer counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility of relying on form comments and identical letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are not generally barred from relying on information contained in form comments; courts have held there is 'no reason the Secretary was not entitled to rely on such letters' and that pooling efforts or identical language does not inherently undermine support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on form letters is permissible, but agencies must still consider whether the substance of the comments raises material issues requiring response; ignoring categories of comments that raise differing views can be arbitrary (Morales v. Lyng example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness and self-selection of commenters
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments represent a self-selected group and are not necessarily representative of the broader public; commenters may disproportionately reflect more privileged groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be cautious about treating comment sentiment as a proxy for public opinion and consider potential biases when assessing the weight of comment evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy consideration: potential need for congressional guidance on weighing comment volume/sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations recommended Congress consider amending the APA to provide guidance to agencies on the extent to which they should consider the volume or sentiment of comments when finalizing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of statutory guidance, agencies must use existing legal standards; legislative clarification could help agencies decide when and how to consider comment volume or aggregate sentiment.
